name: Natural or Manmade? Arranging and Rating Park Scenes
description:
Faithful replication with the paper's own stimuli: Berman et al. (2014, PLOS ONE 9(12): e114572) asked what makes a scene look natural. In Experiment 1 participants arranged 15 pictures of small urban parks at a time on a screen by dragging, so that distance showed dissimilarity (spatial arrangement method, SpAM); multidimensional scaling of those distances gave a first dimension that tracked naturalness. In Experiment 3 other participants rated how natural each of 307 images looked from 1 (very manmade) to 7 (very natural); naturalness correlated with MDS dimension 1 (r = −.84 and −.75 in two image sets) and with low-level features such as hue, saturation variability and straight-edge density. This template runs both tasks with the authors' 307 images from Supporting Information S2 (CC BY 4.0): 207 park pictures in folder "parks", 50 natural and 50 urban scenes in "nature" and "urban". Each participant arranges 4 boards of 15 different park pictures (60 in total, drawn at random), writes what they went by, then rates 60 pictures for naturalness (40 parks, 10 nature, 10 urban, random order). The arrangement is saved per board as image:x,y (0–1 board coordinates), so pairwise Euclidean distances can be computed for MDS; the page also embeds the paper's mean naturalness rating for every image for comparison.

Differences from the original study: (1) the paper used 29 boards per participant chosen with a Steiner system so every pair of 70 pictures appeared together; here 4 boards of 15 pictures drawn at random from all 207 park pictures, so only some pairs are compared within a person and the similarity matrix must be pooled across participants; (2) the paper ran the two tasks with different participants (20 and 14 students in a lab); here the same person does both, arrangement first, online; (3) participants rate 60 of the 307 images instead of all; (4) Done unlocks only after at least 8 of the 15 pictures have been moved; (5) the open question on what participants went by is added (it stands in for the paper's Experiment 2, where another group labelled the MDS dimensions from posters); (6) images are resized to 640 px and boards use a 16:10 area in the browser instead of a lab monitor.
author: Berman, Hout, Kardan, Hunter, Yourganov, Henderson, Hanayik, Karimi & Jonides
